stem: A bag contains 7 red marbles, 11 blue marbles, and 5 green marbles. If one marble is selected at random, what is the probability that it is blue? Express your answer as a fraction.
explanation: The total number of marbles is 7 + 11 + 5 = 23. The number of blue marbles is 11. The probability of selecting a blue marble is 11/23.

stem: A class has 31 students. Of these, 13 play basketball, 9 play soccer, and 4 play both basketball and soccer. If a student is chosen at random, what is the probability that the student plays basketball or soccer?
explanation: Using the inclusion-exclusion principle, the number who play basketball or soccer is 13 + 9 - 4 = 18. The probability is 18/31. The distractor 22/31 results from adding 13 + 9 without subtracting the overlap. The distractor 26/31 results from adding 13 + 9 + 4, incorrectly adding the overlap instead of subtracting it. The distractor 13/31 considers only basketball players, ignoring soccer entirely.

stem: A survey of 200 employees asked whether they commute by train or by bus. Of the 200 employees, 74 commute by train, 53 commute by bus, and 19 commute by both train and bus. If an employee who commutes by train is selected at random, what is the probability that this employee also commutes by bus?
explanation: This is a conditional probability question. Given that the employee commutes by train, the sample space is the 74 train commuters. Of those, 19 also commute by bus. The conditional probability is 19/74. The distractor 19/200 incorrectly uses the total number of employees as the denominator instead of conditioning on train commuters. The distractor 19/53 incorrectly conditions on bus commuters rather than train commuters. The distractor 53/74 uses the total number of bus commuters rather than only those who also take the train.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A random sample of 400 residents from a city with 52,000 residents found that 37% preferred expanding the public library. Based on this sample, which of the following is the best estimate of the number of residents in the city who prefer expanding the public library?
explanation: The best estimate is 37% of the total city population: 0.37 times 52,000 = 19,240. The distractor 148 applies the percentage to the sample size (0.37 times 400) rather than the population. The distractor 14,800 results from an arithmetic error such as computing 0.37 times 40,000 instead of 52,000. The distractor 52,000 is simply the total population, ignoring the percentage entirely.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A polling organization surveys a random sample of voters in a state and estimates that 43% support a proposed policy, with a margin of error of 3.7 percentage points at a 95% confidence level. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this result?

options.text: Exactly 43% of all voters in the state support the policy.
Between 39.3% and 46.7% of the sampled voters support the policy.
It is plausible that the true percentage of all voters in the state who support the policy is between 39.3% and 46.7%.
If the poll were repeated, exactly 95% of the new samples would yield a result of 43%.

explanation: A margin of error of 3.7 percentage points at 95% confidence means the interval from 43 - 3.7 = 39.3% to 43 + 3.7 = 46.7% is a plausible range for the true population proportion. The statement that exactly 43% of all voters support the policy treats the sample statistic as an exact population parameter, which ignores sampling variability. The claim about sampled voters confuses the population inference with a statement about the sample itself. The assertion that 95% of new samples would yield exactly 43% mischaracterizes the meaning of confidence level.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: Researchers want to estimate the proportion of households in a county that use solar panels. They plan to select a random sample and construct a 95% confidence interval with a margin of error no greater than 4 percentage points. A pilot study suggests that approximately 29% of households use solar panels. They initially plan to survey 350 households. If they want to cut the margin of error in half to 2 percentage points while keeping the confidence level at 95%, what should they do to their sample size?

options.text: Double the sample size to 700
Quadruple the sample size to 1,400
Increase the sample size by 50% to 525
Keep the sample size at 350 but raise the confidence level

explanation: The margin of error is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample size. To halve the margin of error, the sample size must be multiplied by 4 (since the square root of 4 is 2). Therefore the sample size should increase from 350 to 1,400. Doubling the sample size to 700 would only reduce the margin of error by a factor of the square root of 2 (about 1.41), not by half. Increasing by 50% to 525 applies an incorrect linear relationship. Raising the confidence level while keeping the same sample size would actually increase the margin of error, moving in the wrong direction.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A researcher finds that cities with more ice cream shops tend to have higher rates of sunburn. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: Ice cream shops cause sunburn.
Sunburn causes people to open ice cream shops.
There is an association between the number of ice cream shops and sunburn rates, but a causal relationship cannot be established.
The study proves that ice cream consumption and sunburn are unrelated.

explanation: This is an observational study, so it can establish an association but not causation. A confounding variable, such as warmer climate or sunny weather, likely explains both the number of ice cream shops and the sunburn rate. Claiming ice cream shops cause sunburn incorrectly infers causation from an observational correlation. Claiming sunburn causes ice cream shops reverses the relationship and still incorrectly asserts causation. Saying the variables are unrelated contradicts the observed association.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A company wants to test whether a new ergonomic keyboard reduces wrist pain among office workers. They recruit 86 volunteers: 43 are randomly assigned to use the new keyboard for 8 weeks, and 43 continue using their standard keyboards. At the end of the study, those using the new keyboard report significantly less wrist pain. Which of the following is the best conclusion?

options.text: The new keyboard is likely to reduce wrist pain for all computer users.
The new keyboard causes a reduction in wrist pain among office workers similar to the volunteers.
There is an association between keyboard type and wrist pain, but a causal claim cannot be made because this was an observational study.
The results are invalid because the sample size is too small.

explanation: Because participants were randomly assigned to treatment and control groups, this is a randomized experiment, which can support a causal conclusion. The causal claim applies to the population similar to the volunteers (office workers), not all computer users. Generalizing to all computer users goes beyond the study population. Calling this an observational study is incorrect because random assignment was used. Dismissing the results solely due to sample size is unwarranted since the study found a significant result with its design.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A university researcher wants to determine whether a new tutoring program improves exam scores. She emails all 1,230 freshmen inviting them to participate; 174 sign up and are randomly assigned to a tutoring group (87 students) or a control group (87 students). The tutoring group scores an average of 11 points higher on the final exam. Which of the following best describes a limitation of this study?

options.text: Because participants were randomly assigned, the results can be generalized to all 1,230 freshmen.
The 174 volunteers may differ systematically from the overall freshman class, so the results may not generalize to all freshmen.
Because the study was observational, no causal conclusion can be drawn about the tutoring program.
The control group should have received a different tutoring program rather than no tutoring at all.

explanation: Although random assignment within the 174 volunteers supports a causal conclusion (the tutoring likely caused the score increase among such volunteers), the volunteers self-selected into the study. They may be more motivated or academically engaged than the typical freshman, so generalizing the causal effect to all 1,230 freshmen is not justified. The claim that random assignment allows generalization to all freshmen confuses random assignment (which supports causation) with random selection (which supports generalization). Calling this an observational study is incorrect because random assignment was used within the volunteer group. Suggesting the control group should receive a different treatment misunderstands the purpose of a control group in experimental design.
